Had this been done without Mars and Bellona, so that there should have been no place for victory, no one conquering where no one had fought, would not the condition of the Romans and of the other nations have been one and the same, especially if that had been done at once which afterwards was done most humanely and most acceptably, namely, the admission of all to the rights of Roman citizens who belonged to the Roman empire, and if that had been made the privilege of all which was formerly the privilege of a few, with this one condition, that the humbler class who had no lands of their own should live at the public expense--an alimentary impost, which would have been paid with a much better grace by them into the hands of good administrators of the republic, of which they were members, by their own hearty consent, than it would have been paid with had it to be extorted from them as conquered men? For I do not see what it makes for the safety, good morals, and certainly not for the dignity, of men, that some have conquered and others have been conquered, except that it yields them that most insane pomp of human glory, in which "they have received their reward," who burned with excessive desire of it, and carried on most eager wars. For do not their lands pay tribute? Have they any privilege of learning what the others are not privileged to learn? Are there not many senators in the other countries who do not even know Rome by sight? Take away outward show,[212] and what are all men after all but men? But even though the perversity of the age should permit that all the better men should be more highly honoured than others, neither thus should human honour be held at a great price, for it is smoke which has no weight. But let us avail ourselves even in these things of the kindness of God. Let us consider how great things they despised, how great things they endured, what lusts they subdued for the sake of human glory, who merited that glory, as it were, in reward for such virtues; and let this be useful to us even in suppressing pride, so that, as that city in which it has been promised us to reign as far surpasses this one as heaven is distant from the earth, as eternal life surpasses temporal joy, solid glory empty praise, or the society of angels the society of mortals, or the glory of Him who made the sun and moon the light of the sun and moon, the citizens of so great a country may not seem to themselves to have done anything very great, if, in order to obtain it, they have done some good works or endured some evils, when those men for this terrestrial country already obtained, did such great things, suffered such great things. And especially are all these things to be considered, because the remission of sins which collects citizens to the celestial country has something in it to which a shadowy resemblance is found in that asylum of Romulus, whither escape from the punishment of all manner of crimes congregated that multitude with which the state was to be founded.

18. _How far Christians ought to be from boasting, if they have done anything for the love of the eternal country, when the Romans did such great things for human glory and a terrestrial city._

What great thing, therefore, is it for that eternal and celestial city to despise all the charms of this world, however pleasant, if for the sake of this terrestrial city Brutus could even put to death his son,--a sacrifice which the heavenly city compels no one to make? But certainly it is more difficult to put to death one's sons, than to do what is required to be done for the heavenly country, even to distribute to the poor those things which were looked upon as things to be amassed and laid up for one's children, or to let them go, if there arise any temptation which compels us to do so, for the sake of faith and righteousness. For it is not earthly riches which make us or our sons happy; for they must either be lost by us in our lifetime, or be possessed when we are dead, by whom we know not, or perhaps by whom we would not. But it is God who makes us happy, who is the true riches of minds. But of Brutus, even the poet who celebrates his praises testifies that it was the occasion of unhappiness to him that he slew his son, for he says,

"And call his own rebellious seed For menaced liberty to bleed. Unhappy father! howsoe'er The deed be judged by after days."[213]

But in the following verse he consoles him in his unhappiness, saying,

"His country's love shall all o'erbear."

There are those two things, namely, liberty and the desire of human praise, which compelled the Romans to admirable deeds. If, therefore, for the liberty of dying men, and for the desire of human praise which is sought after by mortals, sons could be put to death by a father, what great thing is it, if, for the true liberty which has made us free from the dominion of sin, and death, and the devil,--not through the desire of human praise, but through the earnest desire of freeing men, not from King Tarquin, but from demons and the prince of the demons,--we should, I do not say put to death our sons, but reckon among our sons Christ's poor ones? If, also, another Roman chief, surnamed Torquatus, slew his son, not because he fought against his country, but because, being challenged by an enemy, he through youthful impetuosity fought, though for his country, yet contrary to orders which he his father had given as general; and this he did, notwithstanding that his son was victorious, lest there should be more evil in the example of authority despised, than good in the glory of slaying an enemy;--if, I say, Torquatus acted thus, wherefore should they boast themselves, who, for the laws of a celestial country, despise all earthly good things, which are loved far less than sons? If Furius Camillus, who was condemned by those who envied him, notwithstanding that he had thrown off from the necks of his countrymen the yoke of their most bitter enemies, the Veientes, again delivered his ungrateful country from the Gauls, because he had no other in which he could have better opportunities for living a life of glory;--if Camillus did thus, why should he be extolled as having done some great thing, who, having, it may be, suffered in the church at the hands of carnal enemies most grievous and dishonouring injury, has not betaken himself to heretical enemies, or himself raised some heresy against her, but has rather defended her, as far as he was able, from the most pernicious perversity of heretics, since there is not another church, I say not in which one can live a life of glory, but in which eternal life can be obtained? If Mucius, in order that peace might be made with King Porsenna, who was pressing the Romans with a most grievous war, when he did not succeed in slaying Porsenna, but slew another by mistake for him, reached forth his right hand and laid it on a red-hot altar, saying that many such as he saw him to be had conspired for his destruction, so that Porsenna, terrified at his daring, and at the thought of a conspiracy of such as he, without any delay recalled all his warlike purposes, and made peace;--if, I say, Mucius did this, who shall speak of his meritorious claims to the kingdom of heaven, if for it he may have given to the flames not one hand, but even his whole body, and that not by his own spontaneous act, but because he was persecuted by another? If Curtius, spurring on his steed, threw himself all armed into a precipitous gulf, obeying the oracles of their gods, which had commanded that the Romans should throw into that gulf the best thing which they possessed, and they could only understand thereby that, since they excelled in men and arms, the gods had commanded that an armed man should be cast headlong into that destruction;--if he did this, shall we say that that man has done a great thing for the eternal city who may have died by a like death, not, however, precipitating himself spontaneously into a gulf, but having suffered this death at the hands of some enemy of his faith, more especially when he has received from his Lord, who is also King of his country, a more certain oracle, "Fear not them who kill the body, but cannot kill the soul?"[214] If the Decii dedicated themselves to death, consecrating themselves in a form of words, as it were, that falling, and pacifying by their blood the wrath of the gods, they might be the means of delivering the Roman army;--if they did this, let not the holy martyrs carry themselves proudly, as though they had done some meritorious thing for a share in that country where are eternal life and felicity, if even to the shedding of their blood, loving not only the brethren for whom it was shed, but, according as had been commanded them, even their enemies by whom it was being shed, they have vied with one another in faith of love and love of faith. If Marcus Pulvillus, when engaged in dedicating a temple to Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva, received with such indifference the false intelligence which was brought to him of the death of his son, with the intention of so agitating him that he should go away, and thus the glory of dedicating the temple should fall to his colleague;--if he received that intelligence with such indifference that he even ordered that his son should be cast out unburied, the love of glory having overcome in his heart the grief of bereavement, how shall any one affirm that he has done a great thing for the preaching of the gospel, by which the citizens of the heavenly city are delivered from divers errors, and gathered together from divers wanderings, to whom his Lord has said, when anxious about the burial of his father, "Follow me, and let the dead bury their dead?"[215] Regulus, in order not to break his oath, even with his most cruel enemies, returned to them from Rome itself, because (as he is said to have replied to the Romans when they wished to retain him) he could not have the dignity of an honourable citizen at Rome after having been a slave to the Africans, and the Carthaginians put him to death with the utmost tortures, because he had spoken against them in the senate. If Regulus acted thus, what tortures are not to be despised for the sake of good faith toward that country to whose beatitude faith itself leads? Or what will a man have rendered to the Lord for all He has bestowed upon him, if, for the faithfulness he owes to Him, he shall have suffered such things as Regulus suffered at the hands of his most ruthless enemies for the good faith which he owed to them? And how shall a Christian dare vaunt himself of his voluntary poverty, which he has chosen in order that during the pilgrimage of this life he may walk the more disencumbered on the way which leads to the country where the true riches are, even God Himself;--how, I say, shall he vaunt himself for this, when he hears or reads that Lucius Valerius, who died when he was holding the office of consul, was so poor that his funeral expenses were paid with money collected by the people?--or when he hears that Quintius Cincinnatus, who, possessing only four acres of land, and cultivating them with his own hands, was taken from the plough to be made dictator,--an office more honourable even than that of consul,--and that, after having won great glory by conquering the enemy, he preferred notwithstanding to continue in his poverty? Or how shall he boast of having done a great thing, who has not been prevailed upon by the offer of any reward of this world to renounce his connection with that heavenly and eternal country, when he hears that Fabricius could not be prevailed on to forsake the Roman city by the great gifts offered to him by Pyrrhus king of the Epirots, who promised him the fourth part of his kingdom, but preferred to abide there in his poverty as a private individual? For if, when their republic,--that is, the interest of the people, the interest of the country, the common interest,--was most prosperous and wealthy, they themselves were so poor in their own houses, that one of them, who had already been twice a consul, was expelled from that senate of poor men by the censor, because he was discovered to possess ten pounds weight of silver-plate,--since, I say, those very men by whose triumphs the public treasury was enriched were so poor, ought not all Christians, who make common property of their riches with a far nobler purpose, even that (according to what is written in the Acts of the Apostles) they may distribute to each one according to his need, and that no one may say that anything is his own, but that all things may be their common possession,[216]--ought they not to understand that they should not vaunt themselves, because they do that to obtain the society of angels, when those men did well-nigh the same thing to preserve the glory of the Romans?

How could these, and whatever like things are found in the Roman history, have become so widely known, and have been proclaimed by so great a fame, had not the Roman empire, extending far and wide, been raised to its greatness by magnificent successes? Wherefore, through that empire, so extensive and of so long continuance, so illustrious and glorious also through the virtues of such great men, the reward which they sought was rendered to their earnest aspirations, and also examples are set before us, containing necessary admonition, in order that we may be stung with shame if we shall see that we have not held fast those virtues for the sake of the most glorious city of God, which are, in whatever way, resembled by those virtues which they held fast for the sake of the glory of a terrestrial city, and that, too, if we shall feel conscious that we have held them fast, we may not be lifted up with pride, because, as the apostle says, "The sufferings of the present time are not worthy to be compared to the glory which shall be revealed in us."[217] But so far as regards human and temporal glory, the lives of these ancient Romans were reckoned sufficiently worthy. Therefore, also, we see, in the light of that truth which, veiled in the Old Testament, is revealed in the New, namely, that it is not in view of terrestrial and temporal benefits, which divine providence grants promiscuously to good and evil, that God is to be worshipped, but in view of eternal life, everlasting gifts, and of the society of the heavenly city itself;--in the light of this truth we see that the Jews were most righteously given as a trophy to the glory of the Romans; for we see that these Romans, who rested on earthly glory, and sought to obtain it by virtues, such as they were, conquered those who, in their great depravity, slew and rejected the giver of true glory, and of the eternal city.

19. _Concerning the difference between true glory and the desire of domination._

There is assuredly a difference between the desire of human glory and the desire of domination; for, though he who has an overweening delight in human glory will be also very prone to aspire earnestly after domination, nevertheless they who desire the true glory even of human praise strive not to displease those who judge well of them. For there are many good moral qualities, of which many are competent judges, although they are not possessed by many; and by those good moral qualities those men press on to glory, honour, and domination, of whom Sallust says, "But they press on by the true way."

But whosoever, without possessing that desire of glory which makes one fear to displease those who judge his conduct, desires domination and power, very often seeks to obtain what he loves by most open crimes. Therefore he who desires glory presses on to obtain it either by the true way, or certainly by deceit and artifice, wishing to appear good when he is not. Therefore to him who possesses virtues it is a great virtue to despise glory; for contempt of it is seen by God, but is not manifest to human judgment. # A Close Reading of Augustine's *The City of God*, Volume I

---

## 1. What Happens, Scene by Scene

The text opens not with narrative but with paratext: a title page and detailed editorial matter. Marcus Dods, the Victorian translator and editor, supplies a substantial preface in which he frames the work's genesis. The immediate occasion is the sack of Rome by the Goths under Alaric in 410 CE, an event that pagans blamed on Christianity. Dods explains that Augustine undertook *The City of God* at the urging of his friend Marcellinus, and that the work grew from a few letters into a twenty-two-book monument composed over thirteen years (413–426 CE). Dods surveys the work's intellectual ambition—Augustine's aim is not merely to defend Christianity apologetically but to construct nothing less than "the first real effort to produce a philosophy of history." He notes that the work's influence was immense, its popularity measurable by the fact that between 1467 and the end of the fifteenth century, twenty editions were printed. Dods also acknowledges the work's difficulties: its digressive structure, its occasional use of arguments "plus ingenieux que solides" (more ingenious than solid), and its engagement with now-obscure philosophical and theological controversies. The preface closes with a brief account of the translation's provenance, acknowledging its debts to the Benedictine edition and to Vives' commentary.

The text then shifts abruptly into *Book First* proper, which opens with a dedication. Augustine addresses it to Marcellinus, stating that he will defend "the glorious city of God" against those who prefer their own gods to its Founder. He frames the work's two-part architecture: the first five books refute those who hold that polytheistic worship is necessary for worldly prosperity and that Christianity's prohibition of it caused Rome's calamities; the subsequent five address those who admit that calamities befall everyone but maintain that pagan worship benefits the afterlife. The remaining twelve books constitute Augustine's own constructive theology of the two cities.

The argument of *Book First* unfolds in a series of rhetorical moves. Augustine begins (Chapter 1) with a striking reversal: the very barbarians who sacked Rome "spared those who were found to have fled for sanctuary to the temples of their gods." The Christians who took refuge in churches dedicated to Christ were protected, while those who relied on pagan sanctuaries were slaughtered. The barbarians' respect for Christ—not their own ferocity—saved lives. Augustine asks the pagans: "Why do they attribute it to their own good luck? They ought rather… to attribute the severities… to that divine providence which is wont to reform the depraved manners of men by chastisement."

In Chapter 2, Augustine turns to the authority of literary testimony. He cites Virgil's *Aeneid* to show that even pagan poetry acknowledges the gods' helplessness: Juno is hostile to Troy, and the gods are called "conquered" (*convictos*). If Virgil—who, Augustine notes, is read by Roman schoolboys as "the most famous and approved of all poets"—admits that the gods were vanquished, how could Rome's gods have protected Rome? The poet's own words in Book II are quoted: "Lo! Panthus, 'scaped from death by flight, / Priest of Apollo on the height, / His conquered gods with trembling hands / He bears." For Augustine, this is not metaphor but confession.

Chapter 3 presses the irony further. The Romans delighted in entrusting their city to these gods whom Virgil himself depicts as conquered. Augustine asks: "What madness is it to suppose that Rome had been wisely entrusted to these guardians, and could not have been taken unless it had lost them?" He distinguishes between the gods and their defenders: the men who guarded Minerva's statue preserved it, not the reverse. "How, then, was she invoked to defend the city and the citizens, she who could not defend her own defenders?"

Chapters 4–7 expand the argument through comparison. Augustine contrasts the sanctuary of Juno in Troy, into which Greek victors drove their captives to be divided as spoils, with the churches of Christ, into which barbarian enemies led captives to be set free. He cites Julius Caesar's testimony (via Sallust) that the universal custom in sacking cities was slaughter, plunder, and enslavement. The novelty at Rome's sack was that the largest churches were filled with people given quarter, "and that in them none were slain, from them none forcibly dragged." He asks: "Whoever does not see that this is to be attributed to the name of Christ?" The comparison extends to the historical record of Roman generals like Marcus Marcellus at Syracuse, who wept over the city he conquered but issued no order that those fleeing to temples should be spared.

Chapter 8 turns to a harder question: why do the ungodly share in God's temporal mercies? Augustine's answer is theological: God's common grace—"He maketh His sun to rise on the evil and on the good"—serves a pedagogical purpose. If prosperity went only to the righteous, faith would be venal; if adversity touched only the wicked, providence would seem absent. "The same fire causes gold to glow brightly, and chaff to smoke." The shared experience of calamity and well-being prevents the righteous from "too eagerly covet[ing] the things which wicked men are seen equally to enjoy."

Chapter 9 addresses why the good suffer alongside the bad. Augustine proposes several reasons. First, the good have sins of their own—"every man… yields in some points to the lust of the flesh." Second, the good often fail to rebuke the wicked from cowardice, worldly cowardice, or the love of flattery. Third, some suffering is probation—the case of Job exemplifies that the human spirit may be "proved… that it may be manifested with what fortitude of pious trust… it cleaves to God."

Chapter 10 shifts to the question of loss. The faithful "lost all they had"—but what did they lose? Augustine distinguishes between external goods and "the wealth of Christians": faith, godliness, "the possessions of the hidden man of the heart." He quotes 1 Timothy 6:6–10 at length: "Godliness with contentment is great gain." The apostolic teaching is that attachment to earthly possessions is the root of all evil. He introduces the example of Paulinus of Nola, bishop of Nola, who "voluntarily abandoned vast wealth" and, when the barbarians sacked Nola and took him prisoner, silently prayed, "O Lord, let me not be troubled for gold and silver, for where all my treasure is Thou knowest." His treasure was in heaven, so he had nothing to fear. Some Christians were tortured to force surrender of wealth—Augustine says these "were not good men" if they preferred torture to compliance, for they should have recognized that suffering for Christ teaches the right use of possessions.

Chapter 11 addresses fear of death. "No one has ever died who was not destined to die some time." The end of life equalizes all. "That death is not to be judged an evil which is the end of a good life; for death becomes evil only by the retribution which follows it." He argues that the "dreaded deaths" inflict no real harm on those who lived well.

Chapter 12 takes up the denial of burial. Augustine bids the faithful not be "appalled by so ill-omened a circumstance." Christ has promised that not a hair of the head shall perish. "The Truth would nowise have said, 'Fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul,' if anything… that an enemy could do to the body of the slain could be detrimental to the future life." He cites Psalm 79:2–3 (the bodies of God's servants given to the fowls of heaven) and counters: "Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of His saints." The rich man's burial in purple and fine linen is less honored before God than Lazarus, whose sores the dogs licked. Even pagan philosophers (he cites Diogenes and his followers) "despised a careful burial." The point is that the body's fate is irrelevant to the soul's destiny.

Chapter 13 nuance this: burial is not to be despised, for "the bodies of the dead are not on this account to be despised and left unburied." The bodies of the righteous are "used by the Holy Ghost as His organs and instruments for all good works." The patriarchs were buried piously, Tobit buried the dead and was commended, Christ praised the woman who anointed His body for burial. These are testimonies to God's providence extending even to dead bodies, and they "cherish faith in the resurrection."

Chapter 14 turns to captivity. The three Hebrew youths were captives; Daniel was a captive; Jonah was in the belly of a monster. "God, the comforter, did not fail them." Even in the belly of a monster, the prophet was not abandoned. Augustine notes that while pagans believe the legend of Arion of Methymna, who was carried to shore on a dolphin, they ridicule the story of Jonah—"a story far more incredible because a greater exhibition of power."

Chapter 15 introduces Marcus Attilius Regulus as a counter-example. Regulus, a Roman general captured by the Carthaginians, was sent to Rome on parole to negotiate a prisoner exchange. He convinced the Senate to refuse the exchange, then voluntarily returned to Carthage, where he was tortured to death in a box lined with sharpened nails. Augustine asks: if the gods whom Regulus worshipped "either willed or permitted these punishments to be inflicted on one who kept his oath to them," what does this reveal? Either the gods are impotent, or they are unjust. Regulus "preferred to lose all such things [temporal goods] rather than offend the gods by whom he had sworn." But his virtue brought him no temporal salvation. Augustine concludes: if one righteous man could suffer so under the pagans' own gods, why blame Christianity for the suffering of Christian captives?

Chapter 16 addresses the violation of consecrated virgins in captivity. Augustine's treatment is careful and pastoral. He argues that "the virtue which makes the life good has its throne in the soul," and "while the will remains firm and unshaken, nothing that another person does with the body… is any fault of the person who suffers it." Shame accompanies such violation, but shame is not complicity.

Chapter 17 confronts the question of suicide committed through fear of dishonor. Augustine prohibits it absolutely. The case of Judas is invoked: "by despairing of God's mercy in his sorrow that wrought death, he left to himself no place for a healing penitence." Self-killing is homicide—"he who kills himself is a homicide, and so much the guiltier of his own death, as he was more innocent of that offence for which he doomed himself to die." Lucretia, the noble Roman matron who killed herself after being violated by Tarquin's son, is examined in Chapter 19. Augustine quotes a declamation on her case: "Here was a marvel: there were two, and only one committed adultery." The sin was Sextus Tarquinius', not Lucretia's. Yet she killed herself for shame. Augustine asks: "If she was adulterous, why praise her? if chaste, why slay her?" The Christian women who suffered similarly "declined to avenge upon themselves the guilt of others, and so add crimes of their own to those crimes in which they had no share."

Chapters 20–27 develop the moral theology of self-defense and endurance. Augustine argues that no scriptural passage permits suicide in any circumstance—"in no passage of the holy canonical books… can there be found either divine precept or permission to take away our own life." The Fifth Commandment ("Thou shalt not kill") prohibits killing oneself, for "he who kills himself still kills nothing else than man." The only exceptions to the prohibition of killing are judicial authority (a just law applied generally) or a special divine commission (as with Abraham and Jepthah's daughter, or Samson). Cleombrotus, who threw himself from a wall after reading Plato on the soul's immortality, is cited as a case of "magnanimity rather than justifiable action." Plato himself would have prohibited it.

Augustine addresses the case of holy women who "escaped those who menaced them with outrage, by casting themselves into rivers." He is cautious: "I do not presume to speak rashly" about whether these women received divine authorization for self-slaughter. The principle stands: "No man ought to inflict on himself voluntary death, for this is to escape the ills of time by plunging into those of eternity."

Chapter 28 addresses the spiritual purpose of permitted violations. The women should examine whether they had been "unduly puffed up by your integrity." God may have permitted the outrage to humble them. "Some most flagrant and wicked desires are allowed free play at present by the secret judgment of God, and are reserved to the public and final judgment." The women are assured that their preservation of chastity in will means their purity is intact.

Chapters 29–35 broaden the argument. The pagans' real desire, Augustine charges, is "to enjoy your luxurious licence unrestrained." He traces the moral decline of Rome from the early republic, citing the censorship of Scipio Nasica, who "refused to agree to the destruction of Carthage, Rome's rival," fearing that without an external enemy, luxury would corrupt the citizenry. Augustine agrees: "The seductions of evil-minded devils had more influence with you than the precautions of prudent men." The theatrical games, instituted by the gods themselves, are the chief corrupter. At the very time of Rome's ruin, refugees from Rome's sack were "so infected with this disease" that "day after day they seemed to contend with one another who should most madly run after the actors in the theatres." The chapter closes with Augustine's announcement of the work's further scope: he will review all calamities before Christ's coming, show that the true God granted Rome its empire, demonstrate that the false gods "rather injured than aided" the Romans, and then address those who worship the gods for the afterlife.

*Book Second* begins with a methodological statement: if "the feeble mind of man did not presume to resist the clear evidence of truth," short discourse would suffice. But the necessity of reply is endless, and Augustine warns his reader—Marcellinus—not to demand "a reply to every exception" taken to the text. He then summarizes *Book First*: the sack of Rome, the mercy shown in Christ's name, the problem of shared suffering, the consolation for violated women, and the refutation of pagan scapegoating.

The substantive argument of *Book Second* turns to moral corruption. Augustine asks why the Roman gods "took no steps to improve the morals of their worshippers." He describes the obscene rites of Cybele, the mother of the gods: " productions so obscene and filthy for the ear… that not even the mother of the foul-mouthed players themselves could have formed one of the audience." The rites were called "Tables" (*Fercula*), as if a banquet were being given for unclean devils. He contrasts this with the philosophic ideal of Plato, who in the *Republic* expelled poets from the city because they corrupted morals. "Plato strove… to persuade the light-minded and lascivious Greeks to abstain from so much as writing such plays; the gods used their authority to extort the acting of the same." The theatrical entertainments, which Cicero and Scipio restrict in the case of Roman citizens (no satirist may slander a citizen, per the Twelve Tables), are prescribed by the gods for the gods' own worship. Augustine cites Varro's classification of theological kinds: *mythicus* (mythological, poetic), *physicus* (natural, philosophical), and *civilis* (civic, public). The *civic* theology is what the Romans actually practice, and it is obscene.

Augustine examines the famous Roman virtue of Lucretia, who, after being violated by Sextus Tarquinius, "made known the wickedness… to her husband Collatinus, and to Brutus her kinsman," then "put an end to her life." He argues that she was chaste—only Sextus committed adultery—and therefore unjustly killed herself. The rhetorical question again: "If she was adulterous, why praise her? if chaste, why slay her?" The answer reveals the pagan contradiction: they honor Lucretia for her chastity, but her suicide was a sin. The Christians who survived violation without self-murder demonstrate greater understanding of true sanctity.

The book moves through a survey of Roman moral history. He cites Sallust on the corruption of Roman manners, quotes Cicero's lament in *De Republica* that "the republic has long since lost the reality" of its former self. He argues that "true justice has no existence save in that republic whose founder and ruler is Christ." The chapter "Of the sons of the church who are hidden among the wicked" (*Chapter 35*) introduces the crucial theme of the two cities' intermingling: "these two cities are entangled together in this world, and intermixed until the last judgment effect their separation."

*Book Third* continues the historical survey. Augustine now catalogs the external calamities—bodily and material disasters—that befell Rome even when its gods were worshipped without rival. He begins with Troy's destruction: "Why was Troy… conquered, taken, and destroyed by the Greeks, though it esteemed and worshipped the same gods as they?" The excuse offered—that Laomedon's perjury angered the gods—is undermined by noting that Apollo and Neptune, as divine builders of Troy's walls, should have foreseen the betrayal. More pointedly: "How could they hate in Paris a crime which they made no objection to in their own sister Venus," who committed adultery with Anchises?

The book catalogs disaster after disaster: the rape of the Sabine women, the war with Alba, the reigns of wicked kings, the civil wars, the Punic wars, the sack by the Gauls. The gods are shown to be absent or impotent throughout. A notable passage concerns Saguntum (*Chapter 20*): the allied city that remained faithful to Rome was destroyed by Hannibal for that fidelity. "Saguntum, faithfully keeping the treaty it had entered into… was besieged, taken, and destroyed by a perjured person." If the gods protected Roman allies, why did Saguntum perish? The conclusion is systematic: the gods "neither hurt those whom they hate nor profit whom they love." Their worship is superfluous.

*Book Fourth* opens with a statement of what has been accomplished: the refutation of those who blame Christianity for Rome's calamities, the demonstration that the false gods are "most unclean spirits, and most malignant and deceitful demons," and the establishment that moral corruption was endemic to Rome even before Christ. Now Augustine turns to the positive argument: the true God, not Jupiter and the pantheon, granted Rome its empire.
